host_plant_animal: Grapevine (Vitis vinifera — primary economic host); olive; persimmon; blackberry; numerous other hosts
us_states_affected: CA — 10 counties including Napa, Sonoma, Fresno at peak; eradicated 2016
economic_impact_usd: $6.6 million federal eradication program cost (USDA APHIS EA 2010); CA grape industry ($3+ billion/year) fully protected; successfully eradicated 2016
inoculum_type: Not applicable — insect pest (larval feeding on grape berries)
quarantine_status: ERADICATED — USDA APHIS and CDFA declared eradication August 18 2016; US now EGVM-free
data_sources: USDA APHIS EGVM program page; UC IPM 2016 eradication highlight; NISIC

origin_country: Latin America (Mexico; Central America; South America — native range)
mode_of_entry: Wind dispersal / likely movement of infected plant material
commodity_pathway: Wind-dispersed ascospores from endemic regions; movement of infected corn debris across borders
port_of_entry: Carroll and Cass Counties Indiana; Bureau, DeKalb, LaSalle Counties Illinois (September 2015 — APS Plant Disease first report)
host_plant_animal: Corn / maize (Zea mays — only known host)
us_states_affected: IN, IL (2015); MI, WI, OH, MN, IA, PA, NY (2018 epidemic spread); now in 20+ Midwest and Great Lakes states
spread_rate_km_per_year: Rapid via wind during epidemic years
economic_impact_usd: $1.2 billion corn yield loss in 2021 alone — 231 million bushels lost (APS/Purdue University 2022); IN alone lost $253 million; 11–46% yield loss in affected fields
inoculum_type: Wind-dispersed ascospores (airborne — primary long-distance inoculum from infected leaf litter); secondary spread by conidia via rain splash; overwinters as pseudostromata embedded in leaf tissue; polycyclic disease in warm humid conditions
quarantine_status: No federal quarantine (established); USDA NIFA funding resistance breeding and fungicide trials
data_sources: APS Plant Disease — First Report US: PDIS-12-15-1506-PDN; Purdue Extension; APS Tar Spot Recovery Plan PHP-04-21-0074-RP; 2021 loss data from Midwest corn production reports

pest_scientific_name: Grapevine red blotch virus (GRBV) — Genus Grablovirus
origin_country: United States — believed to originate in wild North American Vitis germplasm or via unknown introduction
origin_region: Unknown — possibly native US source or introduced via international germplasm exchange
commodity_pathway: Infected grapevine cuttings and grafted planting material distributed through nursery trade across US
port_of_entry: UC Davis Oakville Experimental Vineyard CA (first diseased vines noticed 2007-2008; virus characterized and named 2012)
host_plant_animal: Grapevine (Vitis vinifera; V. labrusca; Vitis spp. — commercial and wild)
us_states_affected: CA (widespread); OR, WA, NY, VA, ID, and most US wine grape regions
spread_rate_km_per_year: Slow natural spread (three-cornered alfalfa hopper Spissistilus festinus is vector); rapid via infected planting stock
economic_impact_usd: $2,200–$68,500 per hectare over 25-year vineyard lifespan (Ricketts et al. 2017, PLOS ONE); US wine grape industry ($4 billion/year) broadly threatened
inoculum_type: Phloem-limited virus — transmitted by three-cornered alfalfa hopper (Spissistilus festinus) in circulative non-propagative mode; primary spread via infected planting material; graft-transmissible; not mechanically or seed-transmitted
quarantine_status: No federal quarantine; voluntary certification programs (USDA Clean Plant Network); management is vine removal and replanting with certified stock
data_sources: UC Davis news — GRBV threat to US grape industry; APS Phytopathology 2015; Krenz et al. 2012 (virus first characterized); economic impact: APS PhytoFrontiers 2022 survey

origin_country: Europe (strain virulence increase; widely established globally but new highly virulent strains)
commodity_pathway: Infected impatiens bedding plant transplants distributed via horticultural supply chain nationally
port_of_entry: Northeast and Midwest US (fall 2011 — simultaneous reports in multiple states; FL landscape/nursery February 2012)
host_plant_animal: Common impatiens (Impatiens walleriana — highly susceptible; entire plant collapses); New Guinea impatiens (I. hawkeri — tolerant); other Impatiens spp.
us_states_affected: Nationwide — all major US landscape and bedding plant markets; most severe in Northeast, Midwest, FL
spread_rate_km_per_year: Rapid via infected transplant distribution and airborne sporangia
economic_impact_usd: $200+ million/year retail impatiens market effectively eliminated in most US markets (Ball Horticultural 2013); Impatiens walleriana was the #1-selling US bedding plant prior to outbreak
inoculum_type: Sporangia (asexual) — airborne and water-splash dispersed; oospores (sexual) survive in soil for years as thick-walled resting spores; primary inoculum from infected transplants; disease cycle accelerates rapidly in cool moist conditions; systemic infection with no cure
quarantine_status: No federal quarantine (established); industry-led transition to New Guinea impatiens and alternative species; cultural and fungicide management
data_sources: UMD Extension Impatiens Downy Mildew resource; Penn State Extension; UF/IFAS — first US reports fall 2011 Northeast/Midwest; FL February 2012

origin_country: East Asia (China; Japan; Korea — native range)
commodity_pathway: Infected Buxus (boxwood) nursery stock via horticultural trade — arrived through Canada (Ontario first North America detection 2018)
port_of_entry: Niagara County NY — larvae collected August 6 2021; adults July 16 2021 (first US breeding population)
host_plant_animal: All Buxus spp. (boxwood); Euonymus; Pachysandra
us_states_affected: NY (Erie, Niagara, Orleans counties — federal quarantine); DE, KY, MA, MD, MI, OH, PA, VA, WV
economic_impact_usd: $160+ million/year US boxwood nursery industry at risk (USDA APHIS 2021); active federal eradication program underway; tens of millions of landscape plants threatened
inoculum_type: Not applicable — insect pest (larval leaf and stem feeding)
quarantine_status: Federal quarantine — Erie, Niagara, Orleans Counties NY; eradication program active; no interstate movement of Buxus from quarantine zones
data_sources: USDA APHIS DA-2022-13 (quarantine establishment); APHIS Box Tree Moth Pest Alert; NISIC

commodity_pathway: Infested potato tubers or contaminated soil on potato propagative material
host_plant_animal: Potato (Solanum tuberosum), tomato, eggplant, and solanaceous weeds
us_states_affected: Limited detection — ID
economic_impact_usd: $2.6 billion US potato industry at annual risk (USDA NIFA/APHIS); potential yield losses up to 80% in infested fields (Contina et al. 2019, Phytopathology); quarantine in ID and WA
inoculum_type: Encysted eggs in soil; cysts can survive 30+ years in soil; second-stage juveniles (J2) hatch in response to potato root diffusate and infect roots to form syncytia
quarantine_status: Federal quarantine
data_sources: Skantar et al., 2007, Journal of Nematology 39:133–146; Hafez et al., 2007, Plant Disease 91:325; Contina et al., 2019, Phytopathology 109:1840–1849; https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant-pests-diseases/pcn

commodity_pathway: Infested nursery stock and ornamental plant material with contaminated soil/roots
port_of_entry: Unknown — first found in Florida nurseries
host_plant_animal: Sweetpotato, guava, tomato, pepper, cotton, soybean, tobacco, ornamental plants (>100 host species)
us_states_affected: FL, NC, SC, LA, GA
economic_impact_usd: Under active assessment — total sweetpotato crop losses documented in NC (NC State Extension 2018); impacts on 40+ host crops under quantification by USDA NIFA
inoculum_type: Eggs deposited in gelatinous matrix on roots; J2 infective stage penetrates root tips and induces giant cell feeding sites; completes life cycle in 4–5 weeks; overcomes Mi-1 and other RKN resistance genes

data_sources: Brito et al., 2004, Journal of Nematology 36:232–240; Ye et al., 2021, Plant Disease 105:2240–2252; https://www.findmenematode.org/what-is-me

host_plant_animal: American beech (Fagus grandifolia), European beech (Fagus sylvatica), Oriental beech (Fagus orientalis)
us_states_affected: OH, PA, NY, NJ, CT, RI, ME, WV, VA, MI

data_sources: Carta et al., 2020, Forest Pathology 50:e12580; Burke et al., 2020, Forest Pathology 50:e12579; https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/terrestrial/pathogens-and-diseases/beech-leaf-disease
